verdict.summary:
NICE GUIDELINE IDENTIFICATION FOR A PRIMARY-CARE HYPERTENSION PATHWAY (ADULTS, INCLUDING ADULTS WITH TYPE 2 DIABETES)

Status: draft evidence summary for review by a qualified clinician. Not medical advice and not for patient care. Documentary identification only — no recommendation text is reproduced and no treatment thresholds are asserted here.
Currency check: all pages cited below were fetched on 2026-11-23 (UTC). Any use after that date requires re-verification, because NICE updates guidelines in place and the answer to ask 1 is version-dependent.

=====================================================================
1. ANSWERS
=====================================================================

ASK 1 — Which NICE guideline covers the scope (identifying and treating primary hypertension in adults, including adults with type 2 diabetes)?
ANSWER: NICE guideline NG136, 'Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management'.
Basis (verbatim, NG136 overview page): 'This guideline covers identifying and treating primary hypertension (high blood pressure) in people aged 18 and over, including people with type 2 diabetes. It aims to reduce the risk of cardiovascular problems such as heart attacks and strokes by helping healthcare professionals to diagnose hypertension accurately and treat it effectively.'

ASK 2 — Which earlier NICE hypertension guideline does it say it updates and replaces?
ANSWER: NICE clinical guideline CG127, 'Hypertension: clinical management of primary hypertension in adults'.
Basis (verbatim, NG136 overview page): 'This guideline updates and replaces NICE guideline CG127. It also updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in the NICE guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults (NG28).'
Corroboration (verbatim, NG136 PDF, p.4): 'This guideline replaces CG127. This guideline partially replaces NG28.'

SECONDARY FACT — recorded so the pathway does not double-count, but NOT the answer to ask 2:
NG136 also updates and replaces only the blood-pressure-management section of NG28, 'Type 2 diabetes in adults: management'. NG28 is a diabetes guideline, not a hypertension guideline, and it is only partially replaced. NG28's own update information states (verbatim): 'August 2019: The recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension have been removed because diagnosis, treatment and monitoring of hypertension is broadly the same for people with type 2 diabetes as for other people (see the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults). When a different approach is needed for people with type 2 diabetes, this is specified in the hypertension guideline.' The NG28 overview page likewise directs: 'For recommendations on hypertension in people with type 2 diabetes, see the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults.'
Practical consequence for the pathway: cite NG136 for all hypertension identification, treatment and monitoring content in adults with type 2 diabetes; cite NG28 only for glycaemic management and diabetes-specific care; do not cite CG127 anywhere as current.

=====================================================================
2. FULL CITATIONS (source of record for each answer)
=====================================================================

[S1] National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG136. London: NICE. Overview page. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (fetched 2026-11-23; page states 'Last reviewed: 26 February 2026').
  Supports: ask 1 (scope wording), ask 2 (succession wording), the NG28 partial-replacement statement, and the note that a separate NICE guideline on hypertension in pregnancy exists.
  Verification caveat: the original publication date of NG136 (widely given as 28 August 2019) is NOT restated in the passages fetched. Confirm on the guideline page before printing a publication date in the pathway document.

[S2] National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG136. Full guideline PDF, 57 pp. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213 (fetched 2026-11-23; footer '© NICE 2026').
  Supports: 'This guideline replaces CG127. This guideline partially replaces NG28.'; 'This guideline is the basis of QS181, QS28 and QS209.'; the scope-of-application statement quoted in section 4 below.

[S3] National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Type 2 diabetes in adults: management. NICE guideline NG28. Published 02 December 2015; last updated 18 February 2026. Update information chapter. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28/chapter/update-information (fetched 2026-11-23).
  Supports: the August 2019 removal of hypertension recommendations from NG28 and the signposting to the hypertension guideline.

[S4] National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Type 2 diabetes in adults: management. NICE guideline NG28. Overview page. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG28 (fetched 2026-11-23; page states 'Last reviewed: 05 November 2026').
  Supports: 'For recommendations on hypertension in people with type 2 diabetes, see the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults'; and confirmation that NG28's current update in development concerns atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity — not hypertension.

Unverified-by-fetch identifiers (named for completeness; verify before use, do not print as fact): the pregnancy guideline referenced by NG136 as 'NICE has also produced a guideline on hypertension in pregnancy' is generally NG133, and the chronic kidney disease guideline cross-referenced in NG136's treatment sections is generally NG203. The fetched passages confirm that separate guidelines exist and are cross-referenced, but do not give their numbers.

=====================================================================
3. WHAT NG136 SAYS ABOUT ITS OWN APPLICATION TO ADULTS WITH TYPE 2 DIABETES
=====================================================================
Verbatim (NG136 PDF, p.5): 'The recommendations on measuring blood pressure and diagnosing hypertension in this guideline apply to all adults, including those with type 2 diabetes. The recommendations on treatment and monitoring link to NICE's guidelines on chronic kidney disease, type 1 diabetes and hypertension in pregnancy at points in the care pathway where treatment differs. The recommendations on treatment and monitoring apply to adults with type 2 diabetes and replace recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension in NICE's guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults.'
Verbatim (NG136 PDF, section on choosing antihypertensive drug treatment): 'The recommendations in this section apply to people with hypertension with or without type 2 diabetes. They replace the recommendations on diagnosing and managing hypertension in NICE's guideline on type 2 diabetes in adults.'
Implication: the pathway needs a single hypertension source (NG136) for adults with and without type 2 diabetes; diabetes status changes linked content at specific points (type 1 diabetes, CKD, pregnancy) but not the identity of the covering hypertension guideline.

=====================================================================
4. CURRENCY / VERSION STATEMENT (as at 2026-11-23)
=====================================================================
- NG136 is the current hypertension guideline and remains in force. Its overview page carries 'Last reviewed: 26 February 2026', with the note: 'We added a new recommendation to offer advice on healthy living to people who have raised blood pressure but have not been diagnosed with hypertension. See update information for more details.' This is a content addition within NG136; it does not change the guideline number or the succession statement, so asks 1 and 2 are unaffected.
- NG136 is under active surveillance: 'We are monitoring the ongoing research on the response to antihypertensive drugs in different ethnic groups that may impact recommendations in this guideline. We will check the evidence when published and make a decision whether to update this guideline at this time.' This is the one place where the underlying evidence base is acknowledged as unsettled; it affects drug-choice content, not the identification question.
- NG28 was last updated 18 February 2026 (medicines for type 2 diabetes: metformin, SGLT-2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, pioglitazone, marked [2026]) and last reviewed 05 November 2026, with an update in development focused on adults with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity. None of this restores or alters NG28's hypertension recommendations, which were removed in August 2019. So the partial-replacement relationship in section 1 is unchanged.
- Re-check point for the pathway owner: re-fetch S1 and S2 immediately before sign-off and at each annual pathway review; if NICE issues a replacement guideline for NG136, both answers must be re-derived, since the successor's own 'updates and replaces' wording would then name NG136, not CG127.

=====================================================================
5. SCOPE BOUNDARIES THE PATHWAY MUST STATE (so the guideline is not over-applied)
=====================================================================
- Population covered: people aged 18 and over with primary hypertension, explicitly including people with type 2 diabetes (S1, verbatim scope statement).
- Not covered by NG136: hypertension in pregnancy — NG136 states 'NICE has also produced a guideline on hypertension in pregnancy'; a separate pathway document is required. Also outside the adult primary-hypertension scope: children and young people under 18, and hypertension with an identified secondary cause, which is not the subject of this guideline's scope statement.
- Linked-out points in the care pathway: treatment and monitoring explicitly link out to NICE guidelines on chronic kidney disease, type 1 diabetes and hypertension in pregnancy 'at points in the care pathway where treatment differs' (S2, p.5). The pathway should show these as branch points rather than duplicating their content.
- Quality standards: NG136 is stated to be 'the basis of QS181, QS28 and QS209' (S2, p.4). Do not infer what each quality standard covers from this sentence alone; verify each before citing.

=====================================================================
6. WHERE THE EVIDENCE IS THIN OR NEEDS CARE
=====================================================================
This is a documentary identification question, not a question about the strength of clinical evidence. The two answers are stated explicitly in the guideline's own front matter and are not inferential, so there is no conflict between sources on either answer. The genuine weaknesses are about currency and completeness, and they are listed plainly:
(a) Version risk. Both answers are pinned to the version of NG136 live on 2026-11-23. NICE updates in place; a future replacement would change ask 2's answer to 'NG136'. Mitigation: date-stamp the citation block and re-verify at sign-off.
(b) Unverified bibliographic detail. Original publication dates for NG136 and CG127, and the guideline numbers for the pregnancy and CKD cross-references, were not present in the fetched passages. They are flagged, not asserted. Mitigation: confirm on the NICE pages before the pathway is published.
(c) Partial-replacement wording differs between NICE's own surfaces ('updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in ... NG28' on the overview page versus 'partially replaces NG28' in the PDF). These are consistent in substance but not identical in words; quote one form consistently in the pathway document (recommend the overview wording, which is more specific).
(d) NICE guidance is written for the English health system. The project analysis records that applicability to the team's jurisdiction is an assumption, not a fact. If the team is outside a NICE-covered system, NG136 remains a defensible reference standard but is not the governing standard; that decision belongs to the clinical reviewer.

=====================================================================
7. PROVENANCE BLOCK TO PASTE INTO THE PATHWAY DOCUMENT
=====================================================================
'Hypertension content in this pathway is based on: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG136. London: NICE; last reviewed 26 February 2026. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136 (accessed 23 November 2026). NG136 updates and replaces NICE clinical guideline CG127 (Hypertension: clinical management of primary hypertension in adults) and updates and replaces the section on blood pressure management in NICE guideline NG28 (Type 2 diabetes in adults: management). Diabetes-specific content other than blood pressure management is based on NG28 (published 02 December 2015; last updated 18 February 2026).'
Do not cite CG127 as current anywhere in the pathway; if CG127 is mentioned at all, it should be only in a supersession note.

=====================================================================
8. BOTTOM LINE FOR THE REVIEWER
=====================================================================
Ask 1: NG136. Ask 2: CG127 (with NG28's blood-pressure section also replaced in part, noted separately). Both statements are quoted verbatim from the guideline's own pages fetched on 2026-11-23; the residual work is bibliographic verification of dates and adjacent guideline numbers, and re-checking at sign-off in case NG136 has itself been replaced.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR QUALIFIED CLINICIAN REVIEW
Subject: Whether 'the research is minimal risk' is by itself a sufficient basis to enroll a subject in an FDA-regulated clinical investigation without informed consent under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21; and the Part 50 definition of 'minimal risk'.
Status: Draft for review by a qualified clinician and the reviewing IRB. Not legal advice. Not for the care of any individual subject. No protocol-specific facts are assumed.

=====================================================================
1. QUESTIONS AND SHORT ANSWERS
=====================================================================

Q1 (verdict). An investigator says an FDA-regulated clinical investigation may enroll a person without informed consent solely because the research is minimal risk. Under 21 CFR Part 50 as in force on 2026-11-21, is that reason sufficient?

A1. NO. Minimal risk is necessary but not sufficient. Since the codification of 21 CFR 50.22 ('Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations'), no more than minimal risk is criterion (a) of five findings that the IRB — not the investigator — must make and document before an IRB may approve a consent procedure that omits or alters any element of § 50.25(a) or (b), or waive consent entirely. An investigator's own conclusion that a study is minimal risk has no operative legal effect and, standing alone, does not authorize enrollment without consent. Separately, in the two emergency pathways (§ 50.23 and § 50.24) minimal risk is not the operative test at all.

Q2 (value). How does Part 50 define 'minimal risk'?

A2. 21 CFR 50.3(k). Verbatim: 'Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.'

3. ANSWER TO Q1 IN FULL — WHY 'MINIMAL RISK' ALONE IS NOT SUFFICIENT
=====================================================================

3.1 The operative provision: 21 CFR 50.22

Section 50.22, as verified in S1, reads in full:

'§ 50.22 Exception from informed consent requirements for minimal risk clinical investigations.
The IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation described in this section may approve an informed consent procedure that does not include or that alters some or all of the elements of informed consent set forth in § 50.25(a) and (b), or may waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following:
(a) The clinical investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects;
(b) The clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration;
(c) If the clinical investigation involves using identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens, the clinical investigation could not practicably be carried out without using such information or biospecimens in an identifiable format;
(d) The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects; and
(e) Whenever appropriate, the subjects or legally authorized representatives will be provided with additional pertinent information after participation.'

3.2 The five findings, and the role minimal risk plays

| Criterion | What must be found | Who finds it | Independent of minimal risk? |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | The investigation involves no more than minimal risk to the subjects | IRB | This is the minimal-risk element |
| (b) | The investigation could not practicably be carried out without the requested waiver or alteration | IRB | Yes — a separate, fact-specific practicality judgment |
| (c) | If identifiable private information or identifiable biospecimens are used, the investigation could not practicably be carried out without using them in identifiable form | IRB | Yes — triggered only where identifiable information/biospecimens are involved |
| (d) | The waiver or alteration will not adversely affect the rights and welfare of the subjects | IRB | Yes |
| (e) | Whenever appropriate, subjects or legally authorized representatives receive additional pertinent information after participation | IRB | Yes — post-participation debriefing |

The structure of the sentence is conjunctive: the IRB 'may ... waive the requirement to obtain informed consent, provided the IRB finds and documents the following: (a) ... (b) ... (c) ... (d) ... and (e).' All five must be satisfied and documented. A finding of no more than minimal risk discharges (a) only.

3.3 Three independent reasons the investigator's stated reason fails as stated

(i) It answers only one of five criteria. Even a correct minimal-risk determination leaves (b), (c), (d) and (e) unaddressed. Criterion (b) in particular is not implied by low risk: a minimal-risk study that could practicably be carried out with consent (e.g., a survey, a single extra blood draw at a scheduled visit, a review of records where consent is feasible) does not satisfy (b) merely because it is low risk. Low risk and impracticability are different questions.

(ii) The finding belongs to the IRB, not the investigator. Section 50.22 confers the authority on 'the IRB responsible for the review, approval, and continuing review of the clinical investigation'. The investigator's own classification of the study as minimal risk is not a legal authorization to enroll anyone without consent. Enrolling on that basis is a departure from the consent requirements of §§ 50.25 and 50.27 and from the IRB-approved protocol.

(iii) The findings must be documented. Section 50.22 requires the IRB to 'find and document'. A verbal or assumed understanding is not sufficient; the investigator should hold a written IRB determination (typically the approval letter and minutes) recording each of (a)-(e) before the first enrollment without consent.

3.4 What minimal risk does and does not do

- It does: make a study eligible for IRB consideration of waiver or alteration of consent under § 50.22, alongside the other four findings.
- It does not: waive consent by operation of law; transfer the decision to the investigator; dispense with any of (b)-(e); or apply at all to the emergency pathways in §§ 50.23 and 50.24.
- Historical note: before § 50.22 was codified, FDA's Part 50 contained no general IRB authority to waive consent for minimal-risk research; the only consent exceptions were the emergency provisions (§§ 50.23 and 50.24) and the separate waiver of documentation at § 56.109(c). Under that earlier state of the regulation the investigator's statement would have been wrong outright. It is now wrong in part — the premise is a permissible predicate but not a sufficient one. Confirm the § 50.22 effective date against the Federal Register (S6) before relying on this history externally.

3.5 The other consent pathways — minimal risk is not the test

(a) 21 CFR 50.23 — emergency use of a test article in an individual patient. Per S2, even in an emergency the investigator must obtain consent unless both the investigator and a physician not otherwise participating in the investigation certify in writing all four of the following [21 CFR 50.23(a)]:
  1. The subject is confronted by a life-threatening situation necessitating the use of the test article.
  2. Informed consent cannot be obtained because of an inability to communicate with, or obtain legally effective consent from, the subject.
  3. Time is not sufficient to obtain consent from the subject's legally authorized representative.
  4. No alternative method of approved or generally recognized therapy is available that provides an equal or greater likelihood of saving the subject's life.
  None of these four conditions is 'minimal risk'. A minimal-risk study cannot use § 50.23, and § 50.23 does not require or permit a minimal-risk justification.

(b) 21 CFR 50.24 — planned emergency research. Per S2 and S3, § 50.24 covers planned research in life-threatening emergent situations in which prospective informed consent is waived; the research must hold out the prospect of direct benefit to the subjects, the research plan must be approved in advance by FDA and the IRB, and additional protections must be included (e.g., consultation with and public disclosure to the communities in which the research will be conducted or from which subjects will be drawn, or both). Per S7 and S8, the IRB applies the § 50.24 criteria and FDA's guidance flow-chart (Appendix C), a data monitoring committee provides oversight, and consent is sought as soon as reasonably possible from the legally authorized representative or the subject on regain of capacity. This pathway is directed at research that holds out direct benefit in a life-threatening setting — the opposite end of the risk spectrum from minimal risk — and minimal risk is not one of its criteria.

(c) 21 CFR 50.23(d) — the Department of Defense / Presidential waiver mechanism. Per S1, this provision operates through a set of DOD-specific standards and certifications (including FDA concluding the IND may proceed subject to a Presidential decision, DOD training of personnel and potential recipients, a justified time period not to exceed one year unless separately renewed, a continuing reporting obligation to FDA and the President, and public notice in the Federal Register). It is unavailable to an ordinary sponsor-investigator and does not turn on minimal risk.

3.6 The most likely source of the investigator's confusion: 21 CFR 56.109(c)

A separate provision, 21 CFR 56.109(c) (S5 — cited from codified text, to be re-verified), permits an IRB to waive the requirement for the investigator to obtain a SIGNED consent form — i.e., to waive DOCUMENTATION of consent, not consent itself — where either (1) the only record linking the subject and the research would be the consent document and the principal risk would be potential harm from a breach of confidentiality, or (2) the research presents no more than minimal risk of harm to subjects and involves no procedures for which written consent is normally required outside the research context. Criterion (2) is the one place in the FDA regulations where minimal risk carries most of the weight — but it still requires the second clause (no procedures for which written consent is normally required outside the research context), and it waives only the signature. The subject is still consented, ordinarily orally, and the consent is still documented in the case record. If the investigator's real problem is that a signature is burdensome rather than that consent itself is impossible, § 56.109(c) is the correct provision, not § 50.22.

3.7 Decision procedure the study team should apply

Step 1. Confirm the investigation is FDA-regulated and within the scope of Part 50 (21 CFR 50.1) and Part 56 (21 CFR 56.101). If it is regulated only by the Common Rule (45 CFR 46), this memo does not control; note that 45 CFR 46.116(f) contains parallel waiver criteria.
Step 2. Is this a life-threatening emergency in an individual patient? → § 50.23, with the four written certifications. Is this planned emergency research in a life-threatening condition holding out direct benefit? → § 50.24, with advance FDA and IRB approval, community consultation, public disclosure and data monitoring. Minimal risk is not the test in either.
Step 3. Otherwise, if the study is no more than minimal risk AND could not practicably be carried out with consent AND (where identifiable private information or biospecimens are used) could not practicably be carried out in de-identified form AND the waiver will not adversely affect rights and welfare AND post-participation information will be provided where appropriate → submit for IRB findings under § 50.22. Do not enroll until the written determination is in hand.
Step 4. If consent will be obtained but a signature is the problem → § 56.109(c) documentation waiver.
Step 5. If none of the above → full compliance with §§ 50.25 (elements) and 50.27 (documentation).

4. ANSWER TO Q2 IN FULL — HOW PART 50 DEFINES MINIMAL RISK
=====================================================================

4.1 The definition (21 CFR 50.3(k))

'Minimal risk means that the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests.'

4.2 Element-by-element reading

| Element | Text | What it requires |
|---|---|---|
| Two dimensions | 'probability and magnitude' | Both the likelihood and the severity of the anticipated harm or discomfort are assessed together; neither alone is decisive |
| Scope of outcome | 'harm or discomfort' | Covers discomfort (e.g., pain, nausea, anxiety, embarrassment), not only physical injury |
| Timing and basis | 'anticipated in the research' | A prospective judgment about the research procedures as proposed, made at review |
| Attribution | 'in and of themselves' | The research procedures are judged on their own risk, not netted against anticipated benefit and not diluted by the risk of the subject's underlying condition |
| Comparator | 'not greater ... than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests' | A relative, not absolute, standard; the two comparators are stated in the alternative |

4.3 What the definition does not do — three points a reviewer must not assume

(i) There is no numeric threshold. Part 50 attaches no percentage, no probability bound, no severity grade and no absolute risk figure to 'minimal risk'. Any protocol or IRB worksheet that assigns a number to the threshold is applying local policy, not the regulatory text.

(ii) Part 50 does not state whose 'daily life' is the comparator. The text says 'those ordinarily encountered in daily life', without specifying whether the reference is the general adult population or the population actually being enrolled (for whom daily life may already involve frequent procedures). This is unresolved on the face of § 50.3(k). The IRB should state explicitly in its minutes which comparator it applied, so the determination is reviewable.

(iii) Minimal risk is a threshold, not a benefit finding. Meeting it says nothing about whether the research is worthwhile, whether risks are minimized under 21 CFR 56.111(a)(1), or whether the risk/benefit relationship is acceptable under 21 CFR 56.111(a)(2). Those are separate IRB findings.

4.4 Where the term is used in Part 50 (verified in S1 unless noted)

- § 50.22(a): 'no more than minimal risk to the subjects' — the waiver/alteration threshold discussed in section 3.
- § 50.51: clinical investigations involving no greater than minimal risk to children — the IRB must find no greater than minimal risk and adequate provisions for assent and parental permission (§ 50.55).
- § 50.52: investigations involving more than minimal risk to children but presenting the prospect of direct benefit — the IRB must find the risk is justified by the anticipated benefit.
- §§ 50.53 and 50.54 (S4, not in fetched set — re-verify): the remaining pediatric risk categories, which are also defined by reference to the same minimal-risk line.

In every one of these uses the term functions the same way: as a threshold that triggers a specific set of additional IRB findings, never as a stand-alone authorization.
